issues.failure_explanation: J is defined as an infimum over the whole solution set S(u), which the paper itself notes may contain several solutions. Theorem thm:properties_C_to_S provides uniqueness of the state equation only within the neighborhoods O(\bar y) x O(\bar p); it does not exclude solutions of S(u) far from \bar y for u in O(\bar u), since a regular (nonsingular) solution does not preclude other steady states. The claim that this theorem implies S(u) = {(y_u,p_u)} is therefore an invalid inference, and it is the only bridge identifying the infimum-based J with the smooth branch evaluation. Consequently Theorem thm:added-1's assertion that this J is C^2 on U_ad cap O(\bar u), with the adjoint-based identities for J' and J'', is unestablished and false in general: if a different solution realizes a smaller or tied cost, J is a lower envelope of branches and need not be differentiable, and nothing in the standing assumptions even guarantees that (\bar y,\bar p) realizes J(\bar u), so the first-order condition written in terms of the adjoint at \bar y can fail.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof asserts that the L^{6/5}-norm of the gradient of the state error is O(h^2) as a consequence of the L^2 state error being O(h^2), via interpolation and inverse estimates. This inference is invalid: inverse estimates apply only to discrete functions, the interpolation-error component satisfies only O(h) (namely h times a W^{2,6/5} norm of the state), and no L^2 bound on an error controls any gradient norm; the natural rate for this term is O(h), not O(h^2). Since the term enters the stability bound for the discrete adjoint difference and is then amplified by h^{-1/2} in the inverse estimate, the correct O(h) bound would yield only $\|\bar{\mathbf u}-\bar{\boldsymbol u}_h\|_{L^1}^{1/\gamma} \lesssim h^{1/2}$, i.e. the rate h^{gamma/2} instead of the claimed (h|log h|)^gamma. The advertised rate therefore rests on an unjustified estimate.
